svg.aria-label: Diagram: what a private CA costs to operate rather than to create, and which choices cannot be changed afterwards. AWS Private CA supports a hierarchy of certificate authorities up to five levels deep, with the root CA able to have as many as four levels of subordinate CAs on each branch. Validity periods nest: a certificate must have a validity period shorter than or equal to the validity period of the CA that issued it, child CAs and end-entity certificates cannot outlive their parents, and the IssueCertificate API fails when asked to issue a CA certificate with a validity period greater than or equal to its parent's, so a subordinate must be strictly shorter rather than merely not longer. The defaults are ten years for a root certificate, three years for a subordinate CA certificate, and thirteen months or 395 days for an end-entity certificate issued through ACM, with AWS guidance that a CA certificate's validity should be two to five times that of the certificates it issues. The central warning is the expiry cascade: when a CA certificate expires, all of the certificates issued directly or indirectly by subordinate CAs below it become invalid, so the expiry date chosen at creation is a scheduled outage for the whole subtree, and revoking a CA has the same blast radius because it effectively revokes all of the certificates issued by that CA. A succession panel records the contradiction between two AWS recommendations: AWS recommends replacing an expiring CA rather than reissuing its certificate, because of the security advantages gained by rotating to a new key pair, but also notes that private certificates issued through ACM cannot be renewed if you replace the CA, so using ACM for issuance and renewal commits you to reissuing the CA certificate instead, which preserves the existing private and public keys. The replacement procedure keeps the old CA disabled, where it still supports revocation for the certificates it issued, until the last of those certificates expires, at which point the old CA can be deleted. A cost panel gives the two modes: general-purpose at four hundred dollars per private CA per month with per-certificate charges of seventy-five cents for the first thousand, thirty-five cents from one thousand and one to ten thousand and a tenth of a cent above ten thousand, against short-lived certificate mode at fifty dollars per month with a flat five point eight cents per certificate but validity limited to seven days. General-purpose is the default usage mode. A table of monthly totals shows one hundred certificates costing four hundred and seventy-five dollars general-purpose against fifty-five dollars eighty short-lived, one thousand costing one thousand one hundred and fifty against one hundred and eight, ten thousand costing four thousand three hundred against six hundred and thirty, fifty thousand costing four thousand three hundred and forty against two thousand nine hundred and fifty, break-even at about seventy-four thousand four hundred certificates where both cost four thousand three hundred and sixty-four dollars, and one hundred thousand costing four thousand three hundred and ninety against five thousand eight hundred and fifty. Billing ends on deletion rather than on disabling, restoring a deleted CA charges for the intervening time, and one clean generational rotation with 395-day ACM certificates outstanding carries about thirteen months of double-running, on the order of five thousand two hundred dollars for a general-purpose CA. A closing panel notes that by default both revocation mechanisms, OCSP and CRL, are disabled, that the key storage security standard default of FIPS 140-2 Level 3 or higher is unsupported in some Regions where CCPC Level 1 or higher must be used instead or the call returns an InvalidArgsException, and that changing a root CA certificate requires updating every dependent operating system and browser trust store because for a private PKI the organization's IT must ensure each browser or system has already added the private root CA to its trust store, otherwise the certification path cannot be validated and clients see errors.
svg.title: What a private CA costs after you create it, and what you can no longer change
svg.text: The create call settles the price, the revocation story and the outage date.
None of the four can be changed later without replacing the CA.
Validity nests, and the defaults stack
Root CA — default 10 years · no pathLenConstraint
Subordinate CA — default 3 years · pathLen decrements
End-entity via ACM — 13 months (395 days)
up to 5 levels · 4 levels of subordinates per branch
a child CA must be strictly SHORTER, not merely not longer:
“greater than or equal to the parent’s CA fails” · guidance: 2–5× the leaf
The expiry is a scheduled outage
“When a CA certificate expires, all of the

text.tspan: certificates issued directly or indirectly by

svg.text: subordinate CAs below it in the CA hierarchy
become invalid.”
Not “cannot be renewed”. Invalid, all at once.
Revoking a CA has the same blast radius:
“effectively revokes all of the certificates issued by the CA”
→ the subtree IS the blast radius. Go wide, not deep.
Two AWS recommendations that cannot both be followed
Replace — “We recommend replacing an expiring CA rather than reissuing its certificate because of the security
advantages gained by rotating to a new key pair.”
But — “Private certificates issued through ACM cannot be renewed if you replace the CA. If you use ACM for
issuance and renewal, you must re-issue” — which preserves the existing keys, i.e. rotates nothing.
The default mode is the expensive one
GENERAL_PURPOSE — $400/CA/month (the default)
SHORT_LIVED_CERTIFICATE — $50/CA/month
certs: $0.058 flat · validity capped at 7 days
certs/mo general short-lived ratio
Billing stops at delete, not at disable
The correct succession keeps the old CA alive:
“While disabled, the old CA supports revocation…
When the last certificate issued from the old CA
expires, you can delete the old CA.”
“You are not charged… after you delete it”
395-day ACM certs outstanding → ~13 months of
double-running → ~$5,200 per general-purpose CA
And delete is not an escape hatch: “if you restore a
deleted CA, you are charged for the time between
deleting it and restoring it.” 30 free days, once.
Three defaults, each defensible, collectively expensive
Revocation — “By default, both certificate validation mechanisms are disabled.” OCSP and CRL, both off.
Key storage — FIPS_140_2_LEVEL_3_OR_HIGHER, unsupported in some Regions → InvalidArgsException.
Root validity — 10 years, and changing it “require[s] you to update all the dependent… trust stores.”
One number decides mode, price, revocation story and succession plan: the longest certificate lifetime you need.
Work it out before the create call, because that call is where all four are fixed.
